
{{distinguish|{{ill|Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|ja|横穴式石室}}}}

[[File:Yoshimi Yoshimi-hyakuana 2.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|en|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|qid=Q11414302|lt=Yoshimi Hundred Caves}} (November 2010)]]
[[File:柏谷横穴群.JPG|right|250px|thumb|{{ill|Kashiya Yokoanabos|en|Kashiya Yokoanabos|qid=Q22118267|lt=Kashiya Yokoanabos}} (February 2013)]]
'''Yokoanabos''' (横穴墓, Yokōbo/Ouketsubo<ref name="rekihaku">{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.rekihaku.city.yokohama.jp/maibun/qa/detail.php?seq=22|title=Q：横穴墓ってなんて読むのですか?|publisher=Yokohama City Foundation for History and Culture|accessdate=2018-07-28}}</ref>) are burial tombs generally carved into slopes or cliffs, typically measuring around 2 meters in height and extending several meters in depth. These tombs served as burial chambers in ancient East Asia and are most commonly associated with the [[Kofun period]] in Japan, where this burial type emerged and became widely used.
== Characteristics ==
[[File:市ヶ尾横穴墓群B群.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Ichigao Yokoanabo Cluster|ja|市ヶ尾横穴墓群}} B Cluster: Forecourt and entrance.]]
[[File:出山横穴墓群 2009.03.21 - panoramio (5).jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Deyama Graves|ja|出山横穴墓群|ja|出山横穴墓群}}: Interior view of the burial chamber.]]
[[File:楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群11号墓.jpg|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Yōkokuji Valley Yokoanabo Cluster|ja|楊谷寺谷戸横穴墓群}} Tomb 11: House-shaped chamber.]]
[[File:長柄横穴群11号墓棺座.JPG|250px|right|thumb|{{ill|Nagara Yokoanabo Cluster|en|Nagara Yokoanabo Cluster|qid=Q17226522|lt=Nagara Yokoanabo Cluster}} Tomb 11: Sarcophagus base.]]
Yokoanabo tombs closely resemble [[kofun]] tombs with horizontal stone chambers. They were carved into rock faces, featuring entrances leading to passageways (羨道, sendō), which open into burial chambers (玄室, genshitsu). These tombs typically lack Kofuns but include exceptions. Burial chambers often feature bases for coffins (棺座, kanza) and showcase various ceiling styles, such as house-shaped, dome-shaped, or arch-shaped. Some tombs incorporate forecourts and intermediate rooms between the passageway and chamber.<ref name="#1">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Keiji Nagahara|editor=Eiichi Ishigami|title=Iwanami Japanese History Dictionary|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|year=1999|isbn=4-00-080093-0}}</ref>
In {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|qid=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}}, Yokoanabo tombs feature the distinctive "Kamakura-type" (鎌倉型横穴墓), where burial shelves or smaller inner chambers were carved into the rear walls of burial chambers.<ref name="#2">{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Sakae Ward Historical Committee|title=The History of Sakae|publisher=Sakae Ward Community Promotion Division|year=2013}}</ref>
Yokoanabo tombs are typically found in clusters (横穴墓群, Yokoanabo bokun). The {{ill|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|en|Yoshimi Hundred Caves|qid=Q11414302|lt=Yoshimi Hundred Caves}} in {{ill|Yoshimi, Saitama|en|Yoshimi, Saitama|qid=Q543313|lt=Yoshimi}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|en|Saitama Prefecture|qid=Q128186|lt=Saitama Prefecture}}, comprises over 200 tombs and is a prominent example designated as a National Historic Site.
Some tombs also feature wall carvings and paintings, often categorized as decorative kofun. Colored embellishments have been discovered in regions such as [[Kyushu]], {{ill|Kanto|en|Kanto|qid=Q3812869|lt=Kanto}}, and parts of [[:en:Tohoku|Tohoku]].
== Origins and Evolution ==
Yokoanabo tombs originated in northern Kyushu around the late 5th century during the Kofun period and subsequently spread across western Japan, including the San'in, Sanyo, Kinki, and Tokai regions by the mid-6th century. By the early 7th century, they had reached the Hokuriku, Kanto, and southern Tohoku regions. The practice peaked around the time of the {{ill|Thin Burial Edict|ja|薄葬令}} before declining in the late 8th century.<ref name="#1"/>
== Name ==
Yokoanabo tombs are sometimes called "yokoana kofun" (横穴古墳), but technically the term "kofun" refers to Kofuns, which these tombs lack. They are often grouped under broader definitions of kofun but differ significantly in their construction and purpose.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
The term "Yokoanabo tombs" became common in the 1960s, gaining popularity among researchers in eastern Japan, whereas western Japan researchers traditionally referred to them as "yokoana." The term "Yokoanabo" is preferred for consistency.<ref name="rekihaku"/>
== Distribution and Notable Yokoanabo Tombs ==
These tombs are found from Kyushu through San'in, Kinki, Hokuriku, and Tokai, with a high concentration in [[Southern Kantō]]. The northern limit is thought to be in northern {{ill|Miyagi Prefecture|en|Miyagi Prefecture|qid=Q47896|lt=Miyagi Prefecture}}.
